King Mohammed named the 1,055-kilometer Tiznit-Dakhla Expressway the "Donald J. Trump Highway" on July 2, a symbolic gesture President Trump acknowledged in a video posted on Truth Social.

Officials plan to erase the bulk of Head Start's 133 pages of rules, including standards for class sizes and health screenings, while adding requirements for English-only instruction and 30 minutes of daily physical activity.

Project 2025 and other conservative groups have long called to 'sunset' the program, though Administration for Children and Families chief Alex Adams says the goal is to slash red tape and shift power to states.

Childcare policy expert Ruth Friedman called the proposed changes a 'massive gutting,' warning that removing performance standards undermines science-backed requirements ensuring children receive essential medical and dental care.

The committee must reach decisions within 30 days based on 11 International Labour Organization indicators; Huang Chi-ya, head of MOL's Department of Labor Standards and Equal Employment, said they "will not rely entirely" on partner determinations.

District Attorney Nathan Hochman warned that "illegal eavesdroppers" will be prosecuted, stating privacy is protected regardless of occupation. Defense attorney Alan Jackson countered that Flores is being punished "for reporting racism inside the Los Angeles Police Department" rather than the perpetrators.

title: LAPD officer charged with illegally recording colleagues' conversations

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent signaled the move during a cabinet meeting at Camp David, Maryland, where his notepad displayed the handwritten directive: "To Do Buy Japanese Yen $5-10 bil."
The Federal Reserve Bank of New York executed the trade through Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, helping the yen rebound to about 157.6 against the dollar from near 164 in recent weeks.

Japan intervened Thursday to address historic lows, with officials posting that monetary authorities maintain "a broad range of tools to address market liquidity needs," including potential FIMA repo facility access.
Kyodo News reported Saturday that the United States and Japan may unveil a coordinated policy as early as next week to address the yen's weakness and deter speculative market bets.

During a Friday Cabinet meeting, President Donald Trump claimed Minnesota's leadership caused the attacks, prompting Democratic Gov. Tim Walz to respond that Trump "knows exactly who is responsible for this attack."

summary: On Friday, the Michigan Supreme Court vacated a key permit for the proposed Enbridge Energy Line 5 tunnel beneath the Straits of Mackinac, ordering the Michigan Public Service Commission to redo its environmental review.

The 6-1 ruling found the MPSC failed to consistently examine alternatives to the project or adequately consider how continued pipeline operation impacts public trust resources, such as the Great Lakes.
Justice Elizabeth Welch wrote that regulators erred by not determining if the tunnel would extend the lifespan of the 73-year-old pipeline, creating further environmental harms.

Enbridge spokesman Ryan Duffy expressed disappointment over the project's long review, while Bay Mills Indian Community President Whitney Gravelle praised the decision as a victory for treaty rights and water protection.
The existing pipeline will continue transporting about 540,000 barrels of oil daily across the Straits while the commission conducts its new review, likely delaying tunnel construction for years.
title: Michigan Supreme Court rejects permit for Enbridge oil pipeline under Great Lakes

summary: On Thursday, Amazon disclosed receiving approximately $600 million in tariff refunds and confirmed it will return a portion to customers where specific import charges were passed on.
Earlier this year, the Supreme Court invalidated President Donald Trump's trade tariffs, forcing the government to reimburse companies that imported goods into the U.S. hit by those levies.

Chief Financial Officer Brian Olsavsky said Amazon "largely absorbed" tariff costs, explaining the company received a "limited" refund because it prepositioned inventory in anticipation of the measures.
Consumers filed a class action lawsuit in Seattle alleging Amazon avoided seeking refunds to "curry favor" with Trump, while major companies like Walmart and Costco also pursued reimbursements.
Amazon hasn't clarified when it will process these refunds, though customers can expect word from the retailer soon as it proactively contacts affected shoppers to automatically issue payments.
title: Amazon received $600M in Trump tariff refunds, will return some to customers

bias: Left-Leaning coverage turns the story into a moral and intra-GOP drama, stressing “brutal” and “gruesome” abuse details, plus Bernie Moreno’s noncommittal “I don’t know,” which it frames as “weak and pathetic”; right-leaning coverage sticks more tightly to the electoral angle, using terms like “flip,” “claims mount,” and “fresh opportunity” to spotlight Democratic gain and partisan turbulence, while de-emphasizing the personal-family subplot.
The key dividing line is whether the allegations are foregrounded as evidence of Republican misconduct or treated mainly as political pressure in a swing-seat contest.
Both sides agree the seat is suddenly vulnerable, tying the split to broader partisan battles over character, power, and accountability.
summary: Facing mounting domestic abuse allegations from his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, Representative Max Miller faces escalating pressure that creates a potential political opportunity for Democrats in his northeast Ohio congressional district.
The legal dispute involves allegations of physical abuse and a broken collarbone on their child; Miller denies all claims and has filed a defamation lawsuit against Moreno to counter the accusations.

Court filings submitted Thursday allege Miller harassed Moreno's attorney, Andrew Zashin, while the House Democratic Women's Caucus and Rep. Shontel Brown demanded an ethics investigation and his resignation.

Ohio Governor Mike DeWine called the accusations "very serious" while noting that Miller's political fate should be determined by voters, even as Republican leaders maintain support for the incumbent.

Democrats sense vulnerability in the district Miller won by 51% two years ago, though consultant Terry Casey suggests opponent Brian Poindexter requires around $2 million to mount a competitive challenge.
title: Ohio Democrats See Opening as Max Miller Abuse Allegations Mount

bias: Left-Leaning coverage stays close to Harris’s court-expansion remark, framing it as a reform idea and even a “popular idea” among Democrats, while the right leans into suspicion, using phrases like “teases,” “controversial,” “packing the Supreme Court ,” and “changed views” to portray the same comments as radical, strategic, and part of a leftward shift.
The right also broadens the story to 2028 speculation and Electoral College overhaul, whereas those angles are de-emphasized on the left.

summary: On Friday, Former Vice President Kamala Harris proposed expanding the Supreme Court to 13 justices while calling for revisiting the Electoral College and statehood for Washington and Puerto Rico at the National Urban League Annual Conference in Nashville.

Harris's recent remarks represent a departure from her 2024 campaign, when she supported Supreme Court term limits rather than expanding the court; she remains focused on the midterms and has "not made a decision" on a 2028 run.

Harris justified her expansion plan by citing 13 district courts as a comparison, while Democrats view court expansion as a way to counter what they see as disproportionate conservative influence over the judiciary.

These remarks sparked renewed debate over institutional reform; Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg previously pitched a 15-member court, while California Gov. Gavin Newsom has expressed varying views on expansion.

Recent consultations with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez suggest Harris is positioning herself closer to the party's progressive wing as speculation persists about her 2028 intentions.
title: Kamala Harris says the US Supreme Court should expand to 13 justices

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the story as a moral indictment, stressing “destruction,” “restrictions,” and “squandering” to portray Canadian aid as wasted by Israeli actions, while right-leaning headlines shift toward a broader, cautionary lens with phrases like “truth behind,” “dangerous,” and “life-threatening mission,” emphasizing aid-system fragility, obstruction, and threats rather than direct blame.

summary: On Tuesday, Jonathan Veitch, head of UNICEF for the Palestinian territories, reported that Israeli water infrastructure restrictions are squandering Canadian aid, citing destruction of the Canada Well facility.

Israel restricts items like cement and generators as 'dual-use' materials to prevent Hamas from building weapons, forcing UNICEF to become the 'provider of last resort' for water and sanitation services across Gaza.

Veitch described dire conditions where families live in makeshift tents surrounded by waste, with nighttime temperatures seldom dropping below 25 C and "millions and millions of rats" infesting the area.
The Israeli Defense Forces stated last week it is assessing infrastructure damage with severity, while 2.1 million Gazans remain confined to 30 per cent of the territory facing critical shortages.

Canada "punches above its weight" in humanitarian assistance, Veitch said, noting private donations helped end a recent famine, though he warned peace remains elusive as thousands grow up without education.
title: UNICEF Official Says Gaza Water Restrictions Waste Canadian Aid

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Fetterman as an awkward fit for Democrats, using mocking phrasing like “hypothetical stranger,” “shitty Democrat,” and “party-breaking” to stress alienation and voter rejection; right-leaning coverage instead spotlights loyalty and principle, emphasizing his “never” vow, “leave Democrats,” and “reach across the aisle” as signs of bipartisan courage.

The key dividing line is Israel: the right treats his anti-“anti-Israel” warning and joint fundraising with a GOP senator as a meaningful test of moral clarity, while the left de-emphasizes those details in favor of ridicule and party drift.
Both sides agree he is unusually independent, but they read that independence through opposing ideological lenses.
summary: Senator John Fetterman of Pennsylvania has established a joint fundraising committee with Senator Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania and refuses to close it despite criticism.
Fetterman stated he votes about 90% with Democrats and denied any plans to leave the Democratic Party, calling such rumors unfounded.
He criticized some Democratic members for supporting abolition of the border, prisons, and the Senate, describing those views as 'full-on communism.'

Senate Majority Leader John Thune said many Republicans would welcome Fetterman if he switched parties, but emphasized the decision is his alone, while Democratic leaders are working to keep him in the party.
title: Fetterman says he would ‘never’ leave Democrats as Senate seems destined for close margins

bias: Left-Leaning coverage was de-emphasized, while center and right framing split sharply over the same sanctions fight: the center presents it as a trade dispute, stressing China “defend itself,” “economic coercion,” and “unfair pressure,” whereas the right foregrounds the U.S. rationale with the “Uyghur forced labor list” and 43 companies.
The tonal divide is clear—neutral denial versus sharper phrases like “malicious measure” and “backlashes,” which cast the clash as retaliation and overreach.
Both sides share China’s rebuttal and supply-chain warning, but they diverge on whether the story is mainly about labor abuse enforcement or geopolitical economic conflict.
summary: China's Ministry of Commerce denied U.S. allegations of forced labour in Xinjiang, calling the accusations unfounded and unfair.

The Ministry criticized the expansion of U.S. trade restrictions on 43 Chinese companies under the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act, stating these actions disrupt global supply chains and harm legitimate Chinese businesses.
China described Xinjiang as stable and prosperous, rejecting claims of forced labour, and urged the U.S. to stop attacks and smears against the region.
The U.S. added 43 companies to the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act Entity List due to alleged human rights abuses, restricting imports linked to those entities.
title: China's Commerce Ministry denies US accusation of forced labour in Xinjiang

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the expiring contract as a moral emergency, using charged phrases like “Five-Alarm Fire,” “abandoning children,” and “deportation targets” to cast the administration as actively endangering vulnerable kids; the right is cooler but still emphasizes risk, highlighting “without a lawyer,” “at risk,” and—distinctively—“many do not speak English” to stress practical hardship and courtroom vulnerability.
The biggest dividing line is whether the story is chiefly about cruelty and blame or about immigration -system consequences and legal limits.
Both sides agree thousands of unaccompanied minors may lose representation, tying the dispute to broader battles over immigration enforcement, child welfare, and state power.
summary: A federal contract from the HHS funding legal representation for roughly 20,000 unaccompanied immigrant children expires today, leaving advocates concerned about the future of legal services for minors in United States care.

The Trump administration has withheld over $65 million in congressionally appropriated funding since late last year, forcing nonprofit advocacy groups to trim operations and refuse new clients as part of broader deportation efforts.
Advocates warn that "fewer than 1% of immigrant children are granted immigration relief" without counsel, forcing minors to navigate complex court proceedings alone.
Service providers, including Acacia Center for Justice, report they "do not know who, if anyone, will take over the work" when the contract expires, creating uncertainty for 20,000 children.

This expiration occurs as Trump intensifies mass deportation policies, while critics point to a record of mistreating unauthorized immigrant children through detention in facilities reportedly plagued by abuse allegations.
title: Thousands of migrant children in the US could face new deportation risks as legal aid deal expires

bias: Left-Leaning coverage foregrounds political blame, casting Trump’s attack on Tim Walz as misguided with phrases like “blames” and “even though it’s probably Iran,” while right-leaning coverage frames the story as a security threat, using “hacked,” “Is Iran to blame?” and “critical infrastructure” to stress vulnerability and caution.

The key dividing line is attribution: the left pushes Iran as the likely culprit and highlights federal warnings, the right insists on “formal attribution” still pending, and the center sits between them with “increasingly appeared” plus a broader Iranian cyberattack timeline.
Both sides share concern over seven-state water system breaches, but diverge on political vs. national-security meaning.
summary: The FBI warned on Friday that cyberattacks have compromised water utilities across seven states, with more than 30 facilities hit in Minnesota alone. This campaign represents the broadest, most disruptive attack on American industrial control systems to date.

A leaked memo obtained by WIRED this week tied the attacks to Iranian-affiliated hackers, confirming an earlier CISA advisory from April. This documentation marks the first official link connecting the Minnesota incidents to a broader industrial control systems campaign.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency stated the attacks disabled digital controls and "resulted in boil-water notices." The FBI and Environmental Protection Agency urged utilities to immediately remove internet-exposed programmable logic controllers and implement allow-lists for authorized devices.

President Donald Trump blamed Minnesota Democratic governor Tim Walz's administration for the security failures on Friday. This partisan response recalled his past denials of foreign hacking , even after intelligence agencies attributed other intrusions to foreign actors.

Federal agencies including the FBI and Environmental Protection Agency are working with affected utilities to remediate the breaches. These incidents expose the vulnerability of industrial control systems that connect digital software with physical equipment in critical infrastructure.
title: Hackers targeted municipal water systems in 7 states this week, FBI says

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the push as a harsh, “breakneck” crackdown that is “driving up” deportation orders, stressing “packing” courtrooms and a “historic rise” in missed hearings as evidence of immigrant harm and procedural strain.

Right-Leaning coverage largely repeats the same facts but leans toward law-and-order implications, using the same urgency markers to underscore enforcement pressure and backlog relief rather than sympathy.
The key dividing line is whether faster hearings are portrayed as reckless coercion or necessary administration.
Center coverage stays closer to a plain backlog narrative.
All sides agree the system is overloaded, reflecting broader splits over immigration and state power.
summary: The Trump administration is packing immigration courtrooms with "mega" master hearings and reducing notification times to clear backlogs, causing a surge in missed court dates and immediate deportation orders nationwide.

Dozens of immigrants' cases are assigned to individual judges daily through the Executive Office of Immigration Review, with more than 1,300 such hearings held in June alone—a nearly threefold jump from the previous June.

As hearing notice times shrunk, the national no-show rate doubled to 40% by this June, according to Mobile Pathways. Deportation orders surged to about 79,000 that month, often deeming asylum claims "abandoned."

Veteran attorney Jaime Diez recently faced almost 20 cases in one day, calling the rapid pace a threat to due process. Other advocates report immigrants receiving deportation orders while confused inside courthouses.

Andrew Arthur, a fellow at the Center for Immigration Studies, calls the strategy a necessary "time-saver" to clear the backlog, though critics warn the compressed schedules risk denying due process and burning out judges.
title: Trump Administration Speeds Immigration Hearings, Raising Missed-Court Orders

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the bill as easing restrictions and “giving doctors the final word,” emphasizing access, patient care, and hospitals turning women away; center coverage stays more procedural, using phrases like “expand reproductive healthcare” while noting both supporters and critics.

Right-Leaning coverage pivots sharply to alarm, spotlighting “late-term abortion ,” “up to birth,” “blue state,” and “fast-tracks” to portray haste and extremity, reinforced by moral language like “gravely immoral” and “mad dash.” The key fault line is whether the measure is healthcare access or a sweeping abortion expansion, though all sides agree it advances to Gov.
Healey amid a broader abortion-rights divide.
summary: On Friday, the Massachusetts Senate adopted legislation loosening restrictions on later-term abortions, sending the measure to Democratic Gov. Maura Healey for consideration.
The bill permits abortions after 24 weeks by removing four specific statutory exemptions and granting doctors professional judgment to determine necessity.

Supporters argue the change enables residents with serious complications to seek care locally rather than traveling out of state. State Rep. Christine Barber noted hospitals currently turn away women, even when a fetus has a lethal diagnosis.

Opponents, including Massachusetts Citizens for Life president Myrna Maloney Flynn, contend the bill lacks safety prioritization and could permit abortions on healthy fetuses. Westfield Republican Rep. Kelly Pease argued the legislation removes existing safeguards.

Since the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade four years ago, the national landscape has shifted, with 13 states currently enforcing strict abortion bans while Massachusetts moves to further protect access.
title: Massachusetts is close to giving doctors the final word on whether to perform late abortions

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the proposal as an “overhaul” of a Civil Rights-era law meant to protect low- and middle-income communities, stressing policy reform and equity; right-leaning coverage turns the same move into a fight over a “weaponized” CRA, with phrases like “left-wing advocacy groups” and “funded” suggesting misuse and ideological capture.
The biggest dividing line is whether the rule is a fair-lending fix or a deregulatory retreat that helps activists.
Center coverage stays more procedural, noting a “rule update” and tighter grant scrutiny.
Both sides agree it is a major Trump-era regulatory shift, but they read its purpose through starkly different ideological lenses.
summary: On Friday, the OCC and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation proposed updating fair lending rules to increase scrutiny on community development grants while easing compliance for smaller financial institutions.

Conceived in 1977 to combat redlining, the Community Reinvestment Act mandates banks lend to low-to-middle income neighborhoods; regulators have sought to modernize these rules for 30 years amid repeated legal and political obstacles.

The proposal eases data collection for banks with under $10 billion in assets and raises the small bank definition to $1 billion, reducing full compliance requirements by 800 institutions to leave only 86 banks fully subject to the rules.

Senator Elizabeth Warren and other Democrats on the Senate Banking Committee claimed the proposal would "gut" the law, while National Community Reinvestment Coalition CEO Jesse Van Tol said the changes would discourage rural lending.

Uncertainty surrounds the rule because the Federal Reserve, which shares enforcement responsibility, did not issue a matching proposal; stakeholders now have a 60-day comment period before finalization.
title: Regulators propose overhaul to law governing how banks lend to low-and-middle income communities
